, et al., published in the journal Science Advances, says that human circadian rhythm genes, as well as the natural circadian rhythm, can vary widely. The study shows that these people have different versions of the so-called "clock genes" that control the circadian rhythm. Researchers compared 482 healthy volunteers who were night owls with 482 day larks, and found that more than 70% of these night owls had a variation in a specific gene, PER3, compared to only 34% of the day larks. The researchers believe that this variation in the PER3 gene may be the cause of the difference in sleep patterns. What's more, this gene variant appears to be associated with an increased risk of certain diseases, such as depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and dementia.
The study also

, a researcher at the University of Turku, published in the Journal of Biological Rhythms, may help answer that.

The study involved keeping track of their biological rhythms for about a month, with participants being woken up and put to bed at specific times, and measuring their circadian rhythms through a process called dim light melatonin onset (DLMO).
The results showed that among those who were able to function during the night, their circadian rhythms shifted significantly, and their biological clocks were less sensitive to the external environment, meaning they could adjust their internal rhythms more easily.
So the key to being a night owl
